title: Table with row and column sums: do the numbers add up?
summary: A matrix of counts with a row-sum column, a column-sum row and a grand total, plus an explicit check that the totals agree. It teaches the habit of reading margins before cells.

media.alt: Table of solved-case counts for three optimizers over four tasks with row sums, column sums, a grand total of 375 and a check line.
media.caption: Reference render with synthetic demonstration data (design-system gallery).

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: Do the numbers add up?
read_the_figure.axes: Rows: optimizer A, B, C. Columns: task 1 to 4. Entries: solved cases (count). Last column: row sums; last row: column sums; bottom right: grand total. Amber lines separate the margins. A check line below states the three totals agree.
look_at: Does each row sum equal its margin? (153, 100, 122)
Does each column sum equal its margin? (75, 74, 70, 156)
Do row sums and column sums give the same grand total? (375)
Which row and which column dominate?
read_the_figure.proves: If the margins add up, the table is internally consistent: no cell was dropped or double-counted. It does not prove the cells are right, only that they are coherent.
if_wrong: Row sums that do not total to the grand total: a cell or margin is wrong.
Margins mixed with data cells in one colour: a total is read as an entry.
Percentages in the margins that do not add to 100: rounding or an error.

terms.meaning: A sum placed at the end of a row or column (a marginal total).
The sum of all cells, which both the row margins and the column margins must give.
One entry of the matrix, here the number of solved cases for one optimizer and one task.
A margin divided by the grand total, as a fraction of all cases.
A computation that must hold if the table is correct, here the equality of the three totals.

remember: sum of row sums = sum of column sums = grand total.
Check the margins before interpreting cells.
Share of a row = row sum / N.
Margins should be visibly different from cells (colour, rule).

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Position gives the row and column; the number in each cell is the count itself, since a table encodes with text. Margins use a stronger fill, bold type and amber rules so that they separate from the data cells. The check line at the bottom is the one place where colour and text together state the result.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: A table is the most exact form and the one to use when the reader needs numbers. Margins answer the questions people actually ask (which optimizer solved most, which task is hardest) without extra arithmetic, and the check turns trust into a test: if any cell were wrong, one of the three totals would differ.

understand.title: Read this reference render
understand.text: Q1: Do the rows add up? Optimizer A: 10 + 42 + 46 + 55 = 153; B: 23 + 16 + 10 + 51 = 100; C: 42 + 16 + 14 + 50 = 122: all agree with the margins. Q2: Do the columns add up? Task 1: 10 + 23 + 42 = 75; task 4: 55 + 51 + 50 = 156. The four column sums 75, 74, 70 and 156 give 375, the same as the three row sums 153 + 100 + 122. Q3: What dominates? Task 4 gives 156 of 375 cases (42 percent), and optimizer A 153 (41 percent): task 4 is by far the largest column and A is the largest row.

understand.title: The must-check list, explained
understand.text: Totals: the margins and the explicit check line. A table without margins forces the reader to add; a check line that is computed, not typed, is what makes a table trustworthy.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: A table is hard to read for pattern: with 12 cells you cannot see at a glance that task 4 is easy and task 1 hard for optimizer A. Margins are not rates: optimizer A has 153 solved cases and optimizer B 100, but that says nothing about success unless the numbers of attempts are equal. Totals that match prove consistency, not correctness. A single big number in the margin can hide an outlier cell.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: A heat map of the cells with the margins as bar charts (a marginal plot); a stacked ledger (F12.4) to show part and whole; a table of rates, solved over attempted. A mosaic plot for two categorical variables.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Add rates (solved over attempted) beside the counts and shade each cell by its deviation from the value expected from the margins.

steps.title: Margins and the identity that checks them
steps.tex: r_i=\sum_j n_{ij},\qquad c_j=\sum_i n_{ij},\qquad \sum_i r_i=\sum_j c_j=N

steps.title: Expected cell under independence (a way to read deviations)
steps.note: Only meaningful if the cells are counts of independent events; for solved cases out of fixed attempts compare rates instead.

worked.title: Checking the margins and one deviation
worked.problem: Verify the grand total of the table, then compute the share of task 4, and the value expected for optimizer A on task 1 if rows and columns were independent.

solution.text: Expected cell and its observed value.

worked.answer: N = 375, task 4 is 41.6 percent; A solved only 10 cases of task 1 where about 31 would be expected from the margins, a big deficit. (Over all cells chi-square is 56.4, but see the caveat on counts.)

analyze.q: The table counts solved cases. What further number do you need to compare the optimizers fairly?
If one cell were mistyped by 10, which checks would fail?

evaluate.q: Does equal row and column totals prove the table is correct?
evaluate.hint: What kinds of errors do not change the sums?

checks.q: What is the check line testing?
checks.answer: That the row sums, column sums and the grand total all agree.

checks.q: Row sums 40, 25, 35. Column sums 30, 30, 40. Is the table consistent?
checks.answer: Both give 100, so yes at the level of margins.

checks.q: Optimizer A has the largest row sum. Does that make it best?
checks.hint: What does the count depend on?
checks.answer: Not necessarily: counts depend on attempts, and the deficit of A on task 1 (10 against 31 expected) suggests it is uneven; compare rates per task.
